data.claim: _catch_up_globs does read_all under log.transaction() once per field (2 per heartbeat) even when the lease already matches the item
data.falsifier: a heartbeat on a live matching lease shows 0 read_all calls at lock depth >= 1 inside _catch_up_globs on unchanged code
data.mechanism: the pre-check compares inside the transaction instead of against the state heartbeat() already loaded
data.probe_output: assert 2 == 0 (seen['locked_reads'] == 2); after the fix: 9 passed incl. globs/revived-lease catch-up suites
data.question: Does a no-op heartbeat catch-up read and fold the whole log under the events lock?

chunk_findings.detail: The new pre-check decides from the `st` loaded before the renewal, so an edit that lands after that load but before the renewal is invisible and the lease is left pointing at the old globs/resources. For example, item `T` is leased by agent `A` with `lease.globs == item.globs == ["src/a.py"]`. `heartbeat()` loads `st`. Another agent then edits `T` so `item.globs == ["src/b.py"]` and appends the event. `heartbeat()` renews `A`'s lease and calls `_catch_up_globs(..., st)`. `_matches(st, "T", "A", "globs")` compares `A`'s lease globs and `T`'s globs in the stale `st` (both `["src/a.py"]`) and returns `True`, so the code `continue`s without taking `log.transaction()` and without appending the catch-up. The current log now has `lease.globs == ["src/a.py"]` while `item.globs == ["src/b.py"]`; the previous code re-read under the lock after renewal and corrected it. If the heartbeat process exits or the next heartbeat is `lease.heartbeat_s` away, the active lease carries the wrong scope, so the change is not behaviour-preserving and contradicts the docstring claim that edits after the load were always caught by this renewal.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/heartbeat.py:_catch_up_globs / _matches

chunk_findings.detail: The no-op test does not actually prove the append lock is not held. `_watch_catch_up` counts only `EventLog.read_all` calls that start while `inside["on"]` is true and while `_HELD` is already nonzero; it does not count `fold`, transaction entry, or any lock hold outside the patched `_catch_up_globs`. Therefore an implementation such as `with log.transaction(): fold(preloaded_state); if _matches(...): return` passes with `catch_ups == 1` and `locked_reads == 0` while still taking the events lock and doing the expensive fold under it. The same blindness applies if `heartbeat()` itself does a locked `read_all/fold` before calling `_catch_up_globs`; the test only watches the catch-up function, not the heartbeat’s total lock hold, so it does not enforce the change’s main promise that a no-op heartbeat takes the lock only when the mark moved.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_heartbeat_catchup_lock.py:43-77

chunk_findings.detail: The mismatch test only exercises globs, but the stated rule is that catch-up must act when globs or resources differ. Both tests pass if `_matches` or `_catch_up_globs` accidentally ignores resources: the matching test has no resource mismatch, and the second test changes only `--globs`. A concrete input that would expose the gap is a live lease whose globs match the item but whose resources are missing/changed; the code should retarget the lease under the lock, but no assertion covers that path, so a resources-only mismatch bug is untested.

chunk_findings.detail: The changed comment documents the stale-snapshot pre-check as safe because `update --globs` retargets a live lease and only a “few milliseconds” load/renewal window is missed, but the runtime decision is still made from the `st` snapshot loaded before the renewal. A resources-only edit — the case the new test at `tests/test_heartbeat_catchup_lock.py:108-113` explicitly says must be a catch-up mismatch — that lands after that snapshot and before `_catch_up_globs` returns makes `_matches(st, ..., "resources")` true, so the catch-up returns without taking the append lock and leaves the lease’s resources stale. The window is not bounded to milliseconds: the renewal itself can block on `events.lock`, and during that block another agent can append the edit; the previous implementation re-read under the lock after the renewal and would retarget immediately. Thus the change is not behaviour-preserving and the newly documented invariant is false.

chunk_findings.detail: The new docstring accepts, but does not eliminate, the stale-snapshot race: `_catch_up_globs` may decide from the `st` loaded before the lease renewal and return without taking the events lock. It claims `update --globs` retargets a live lease, so only a few-millisecond window is missed; that is not a safe proof and is in tension with the unchanged mismatch test, which still expects heartbeat to retarget after a `--globs` mismatch and re-read under the lock. Concretely, if alpha’s heartbeat loads `st` while T1’s lease is lapsed, another agent can run `update T1 --globs j/*` before alpha’s renewal appends. Because the lease was lapsed at update time, the update need not retarget it; alpha’s renewal then succeeds, `_matches(st, ...)` still sees the old matching globs/resources, and the function returns without a transaction. The just-renewed lease is left pointing at the old globs/resources until the next heartbeat, which is a behavior regression from the old path that re-read under the lock and violates the stated rule that catch-up must act when globs or resources actually differ.

chunk_findings.detail: The new liveness guard only skips when the lease was already lapsed in the loaded state at the passed `now`; it does not close the stale-live window. Suppose a lease expires at 100 with `grace_s=0`. `heartbeat()` loads `st` and `now` at 90, then the renewal/catch-up is delayed until real time 110 but still passes the old `now=90`. At 105 another agent updates the item globs; because the lease is expired at that real time, `update --globs` changes only the item globs, leaving the lease globs unchanged. At 110 `_catch_up_globs` calls `_matches(loaded, ..., now=90, grace_s=0)`, sees the loaded lease still live and its globs equal to the stale loaded item globs, and returns without taking the events lock. The authoritative log now has the item globs changed while the lease globs remain old, so the heartbeat has renewed/kept a lease with the wrong globs until the next heartbeat; the previous under-lock re-read would have seen the new item field and retargeted immediately. The docstring’s claim that “a lapsed one … always takes the lock” is false for this stale-live case.

chunk_findings.title: tests/test_heartbeat_catchup_lock.py:43-77

chunk_findings.detail: The mismatch test only exercises globs, but the stated rule is that catch-up must act when globs or resources differ. Both tests pass if `_matches` or `_catch_up_globs` accidentally ignores resources: the matching test has no resource mismatch, and the second test changes only `--globs`. A concrete input that would expose the gap is a live lease whose globs match the item but whose resources are missing/changed; the code should retarget the lease under the lock, but no assertion covers that path, so a resources-only mismatch bug is untested.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_heartbeat_catchup_lock.py:80-98

chunk_findings.detail: The new docstring accepts, but does not eliminate, the stale-snapshot race: `_catch_up_globs` may decide from the `st` loaded before the lease renewal and return without taking the events lock. It claims `update --globs` retargets a live lease, so only a few-millisecond window is missed; that is not a safe proof and is in tension with the unchanged mismatch test, which still expects heartbeat to retarget after a `--globs` mismatch and re-read under the lock. Concretely, if alpha’s heartbeat loads `st` while T1’s lease is lapsed, another agent can run `update T1 --globs j/*` before alpha’s renewal appends. Because the lease was lapsed at update time, the update need not retarget it; alpha’s renewal then succeeds, `_matches(st, ...)` still sees the old matching globs/resources, and the function returns without a transaction. The just-renewed lease is left pointing at the old globs/resources until the next heartbeat, which is a behavior regression from the old path that re-read under the lock and violates the stated rule that catch-up must act when globs or resources actually differ.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/heartbeat.py:_catch_up_globs / _matches

chunk_findings.detail: The new liveness guard only skips when the lease was already lapsed in the loaded state at the passed `now`; it does not close the stale-live window. Suppose a lease expires at 100 with `grace_s=0`. `heartbeat()` loads `st` and `now` at 90, then the renewal/catch-up is delayed until real time 110 but still passes the old `now=90`. At 105 another agent updates the item globs; because the lease is expired at that real time, `update --globs` changes only the item globs, leaving the lease globs unchanged. At 110 `_catch_up_globs` calls `_matches(loaded, ..., now=90, grace_s=0)`, sees the loaded lease still live and its globs equal to the stale loaded item globs, and returns without taking the events lock. The authoritative log now has the item globs changed while the lease globs remain old, so the heartbeat has renewed/kept a lease with the wrong globs until the next heartbeat; the previous under-lock re-read would have seen the new item field and retargeted immediately. The docstring’s claim that “a lapsed one … always takes the lock” is false for this stale-live case.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/lifecycle/heartbeat.py:_catch_up_globs / _matches
